fields.definition: The complete signal path a broadcast program travels from the studio output, through audio processing and the studio-to-transmitter link, to the transmitter and antenna that radiate it to receivers. It is frequently used interchangeably with 'air chain.'
fields.plain_english: It is the whole path a radio show takes from the studio to your radio. The sound moves through a line of gear, one box after another, until an antenna sends it out.
fields.purpose_function: It defines every stage the program signal must pass through to reach listeners, so engineers can design, align, and troubleshoot the broadcast path as one connected system.
fields.practical_application: A broadcast engineer traces the transmission chain stage by stage to find where audio is lost, distorted, or delayed when the station sounds wrong on air.
common_mistakes: Thinking the transmission chain is just the transmitter, when it also includes studio processing, the STL, and the antenna
Assuming a fault heard on air is at the studio, when it can be at any point along the chain
Overlooking gain staging between stages, which causes overmodulation or a weak, noisy signal
scenario_contexts: Commissioning a new FM station and aligning levels through every stage of the chain
Diagnosing distorted audio reported by listeners by testing each link in turn
Documenting the full signal path for a station's technical records

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: The program audio signal delivered from the studio to the transmitter site for broadcast, typically carried over a studio-to-transmitter link (STL) such as a dedicated radio hop, IP circuit, or leased line.
fields.plain_english: This is the sound sent from the studio out to the transmitter so it can go on air. Think of it as the pipe that carries the show to the tower.
fields.purpose_function: It carries the finished program from where it is made to where it is broadcast, keeping the two sites connected even when they are miles apart.
fields.practical_application: An engineer checks the transmission feed for level, silence, or dropouts to confirm the transmitter is receiving clean program audio before it goes to air.
common_mistakes: Confusing the transmission feed (studio to transmitter) with the off-air signal that returns for monitoring
Running with no backup feed, so a single link failure takes the station off air
Ignoring codec delay, which can cause timing problems with backup or split feeds
scenario_contexts: Switching to a backup IP feed when the main STL radio link fails
Setting reference levels on the feed so the transmitter is correctly modulated
Troubleshooting dead air traced to a lost feed between studio and transmitter

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: The practice of continuously checking a station's transmitted output — modulation, signal quality, and transmitter status — usually by receiving the off-air signal and reading modulation and telemetry meters to confirm quality and regulatory compliance.
fields.plain_english: This means keeping an eye on what the station is actually putting out over the air. Staff listen to the station's live off-air signal and watch meters to catch faults as they happen.
fields.purpose_function: It confirms that what listeners receive is clean, loud enough, and within legal limits, and it warns staff quickly when the transmitter or feed fails.
fields.practical_application: An engineer watches a modulation monitor, an off-air receiver, and remote telemetry to spot overmodulation, silence, or transmitter faults and respond before listeners are affected.
common_mistakes: Monitoring only the studio output and assuming the transmitted signal matches it
Allowing overmodulation, which distorts the signal and interferes with adjacent channels in breach of regulations
Relying on a single monitor point with no alarm, so faults go unnoticed
scenario_contexts: Watching modulation meters during a loud live broadcast to stay within legal peak deviation
Receiving a remote alarm that the off-air signal has gone silent
Verifying signal quality after transmitter maintenance

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: The room at a station or transmitter site that houses the transmitter and its supporting equipment — exciter, power supplies, patching, monitoring, and antenna feed — where the broadcast signal is generated and sent to the antenna.
fields.plain_english: This is the room that holds the transmitter and its gear. It is where the signal gets its power and is passed up to the antenna.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the transmitter and related high-power equipment a controlled, secure space with proper cooling, power, and grounding so the station can stay on air reliably.
fields.practical_application: A technician enters the transmission room to inspect the transmitter, check cooling and meters, and carry out maintenance under the site's electrical safety procedures.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Working on or near an energized transmitter without following lockout/tagout and confirming high-voltage supplies are de-energized and discharged
UNSAFE: Ignoring RF exposure limits when working near an energized antenna feed or transmission line
Confusing the transmission room at the transmitter site with the studio control room
scenario_contexts: Performing scheduled transmitter maintenance during a low-listenership overnight window
Responding to a high-temperature alarm in the transmission room
Switching to a backup transmitter after a main transmitter fault

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 (control of hazardous energy, lockout/tagout)

fields.definition: A radio production technique in which a presenter pre-records the spoken links — introductions, back-announcements, and talk breaks — that will play between songs and other elements, so an automation system can assemble them into a broadcast that sounds live.
fields.plain_english: This is when a radio host records their talking bits ahead of time. A computer later drops them between the songs, so the show sounds live even though it was not.
fields.purpose_function: It lets one presenter quickly produce many hours of local-sounding radio, or program several stations, without staying live on air the whole time.
fields.practical_application: A presenter loads the upcoming music log, records each link while hearing the song intros and endings, and the automation system plays the links back in sequence on air.
common_mistakes: Referring to songs or events by absolute clock time, which breaks when the log shifts
Recording links that clash with song intros or endings because the presenter did not hear the transitions
Leaving gaps or dead air between tracked links and the music elements
scenario_contexts: Pre-recording an evening show so a daytime presenter can voice both
Voicing local links for several networked stations from one studio
Recording weekend programming in advance so no live staff are needed

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)

fields.definition: A short weather report segment placed into a broadcast at scheduled points, often pre-recorded or delivered as a live update, and dropped into the program by the presenter or the automation system.
fields.plain_english: This is a quick weather update slotted into a radio show. It can be recorded early or read live, and it plays at set times.
fields.purpose_function: It gives listeners timely local weather at predictable points in the schedule without breaking up the main flow of programming.
fields.practical_application: A producer records or cues a weather insert and schedules it in the playout log, or a presenter reads it live at the top of the hour.
common_mistakes: Airing a pre-recorded weather insert whose forecast is already out of date
Scheduling or labeling the insert so the wrong region's weather plays
Leaving level or timing mismatches so the insert clashes with the surrounding audio
scenario_contexts: Dropping a live weather update into a morning drive show
Scheduling automated hourly weather inserts overnight
Updating a pre-recorded forecast when conditions change suddenly

sources: NAB Engineering Handbook (National Association of Broadcasters)
